content: Postural hypotension, also known as orthostatic hypotension, is a condition characterized by a significant drop in blood pressure when a person moves from sitting or lying down to standing. This decrease in blood pressure can cause symptoms like dizziness, lightheadedness, blurred vision, and fainting (syncope). The underlying mechanism involves insufficient compensatory responses by the autonomic nervous system and cardiovascular system to maintain cerebral blood flow during posture changes. When standing, gravity causes blood to pool in the lower body, normally prompting increased heart rate and vasoconstriction to maintain blood pressure. In postural hypotension, these reflexes are impaired or overwhelmed, leading to reduced cerebral perfusion and symptoms. The condition can be caused by dehydration, certain medications (such as diuretics and antihypertensives), neurological disorders affecting autonomic function (like Parkinson’s disease), or age-related physiological changes. Diagnosis typically involves measuring blood pressure and heart rate while changing posture, sometimes supplemented by autonomic testing. Management includes identifying and treating underlying causes, medication adjustments, hydration, compression stockings, and physical counter-maneuvers. Lifestyle modifications such as slowly changing positions, adequate fluid intake, and avoiding triggers are important. While postural hypotension can lead to dangerous falls, appropriate management improves quality of life and safety. This module covers the definition, physiology, causes, symptoms, evaluation, treatment options, common misconceptions, safety considerations, and practical guidance to help consumers and healthcare providers understand and manage this condition effectively.

chunk_title: Definition and Diagnostic Criteria of Postural Hypotension
content: Postural hypotension, also called orthostatic hypotension, is identified by a measurable drop in blood pressure upon standing. According to professional guidelines, this is a decrease in systolic blood pressure of 20 mm Hg or more, or diastolic blood pressure of 10 mm Hg or more, within three minutes of changing posture from lying or sitting to standing. This blood pressure drop is often accompanied by symptoms such as dizziness, lightheadedness, or fainting due to reduced cerebral blood flow. Diagnosis is primarily clinical and involves orthostatic vital sign measurements. Confirming the diagnosis requires careful blood pressure monitoring using a manual or automated device, ideally after the patient has been resting supine for five minutes and again after standing. This section provides detailed insights into these diagnostic standards and their clinical application.

chunk_title: Physiology and Mechanisms Underlying Postural Hypotension
content: Maintaining stable blood pressure during postural changes depends on rapid cardiovascular adjustments controlled by the autonomic nervous system. Normally, standing causes blood to pool in the lower extremities due to gravity, decreasing venous return to the heart and temporarily lowering cardiac output. Baroreceptors in the carotid sinus and aortic arch detect this change and trigger reflex responses: increased heart rate (tachycardia), vasoconstriction of peripheral vessels, and increased cardiac contractility. In postural hypotension, these reflexes fail or are insufficient due to autonomic dysfunction, volume depletion, or medication effects, leading to inadequate cerebral perfusion and resulting symptoms. This section explains these complex physiological processes in detail to elucidate why blood pressure falls during posture changes.

chunk_title: Common Causes and Risk Factors of Postural Hypotension
content: Postural hypotension arises from multiple causes. Primary causes include dehydration or volume depletion (due to vomiting, diarrhea, or diuretics), autonomic nervous system disorders (such as Parkinson’s disease, multiple system atrophy, diabetic neuropathy), cardiac causes (heart failure, arrhythmias), and medication side effects (antihypertensives, antidepressants). Older adults are at increased risk due to less efficient autonomic reflexes and higher comorbidity rates. Other risk factors include prolonged bed rest, anemia, and endocrinopathies such as adrenal insufficiency. Thorough history-taking and clinical assessment help identify contributing factors to tailor management.

content: Symptoms commonly associated with postural hypotension include dizziness, lightheadedness, blurred or tunnel vision, weakness, fatigue, and in severe cases, syncope or near-fainting. These symptoms typically occur within seconds to minutes after standing and often resolve after sitting or lying down. Some patients may have multiple episodes leading to falls and injury, especially in older adults. Awareness of these symptoms aids early recognition and intervention to prevent complications.

content: The evaluation of suspected postural hypotension includes measuring blood pressure and heart rate while the patient is supine, immediately upon standing, and after standing for up to three minutes to assess for delayed drops. Additional tests may include tilt-table testing, autonomic function testing, and laboratory assessments to identify underlying causes such as anemia or electrolyte imbalances. Medication review is critical. Clinical evaluation also screens for contributing neurological or cardiovascular conditions. This section details protocols and tools used to confirm diagnosis and guide management.

content: Treatment targets the underlying cause where possible. General strategies include correcting volume depletion through increased fluid and salt intake, medication adjustment or withdrawal of offending drugs, and use of compression stockings to reduce venous pooling. Pharmacologic options like midodrine, fludrocortisone, or droxidopa may be used in refractory cases under medical supervision. Physical counter-maneuvers such as leg crossing and muscle tensing during position changes can help manage symptoms. Multidisciplinary approaches often improve outcomes. This section presents evidence-based treatment options and considerations.

content: Managing lifestyle factors plays a critical role in reducing symptoms of postural hypotension. Recommendations include rising slowly from sitting or lying positions to standing to allow blood pressure adjustment, avoiding excessive heat exposure which can cause vasodilation, maintaining adequate hydration, and regular physical activity tailored to the individual's capabilities. Using supportive measures such as compression garments and avoiding alcohol can also be beneficial. Educating patients on symptom recognition and fall prevention enhances safety. This section provides actionable advice for consumers and caregivers.
